name: Sclerosing stromal tumour of the ovary

reference.source: WHO Classification of Female Genital Tumours
clinicalPearls: A rare benign sex cord-stromal tumour that characteristically arises in adolescents and women in their second and third decades
Almost always unilateral and benign, presenting with menstrual irregularity, pelvic pain, or an incidentally detected adnexal mass
Can be hormonally active and oestrogenic, and cases arising in pregnancy may present with more pronounced hormonal effects
Histology shows a distinctive pseudolobular architecture, with cellular nodules separated by oedematous or densely sclerotic hypocellular tissue
A prominent, often haemangiopericytoma-like vascular network and admixed spindle and rounded (sometimes signet-ring-like) cells are typical
Imaging frequently shows early peripheral enhancement with centripetal fill-in, reflecting the rich vascularity
Cured by conservative surgery, and fertility-sparing cystectomy or oophorectomy is usually appropriate given the young age group
reference.pathophysiology: Sclerosing stromal tumour is a benign ovarian sex cord-stromal neoplasm characterised by a pseudolobular growth pattern in which cellular areas alternate with hypocellular, oedematous, or collagenised sclerotic zones. The cellular regions contain a mixture of spindled fibroblast-like cells and rounded cells with vacuolated, lipid-laden cytoplasm, and a conspicuous thin-walled branching vasculature reminiscent of a haemangiopericytoma. Some of the vacuolated cells can produce steroids, which accounts for the oestrogenic manifestations seen in a proportion of patients, particularly during pregnancy when hormonal activity may be accentuated. Despite a sometimes alarming cellularity and rich vascular pattern, the tumour behaves in a uniformly benign fashion.
additionalInvestigations: Transvaginal ultrasound to characterise a solid or mixed adnexal mass and its vascularity
Pelvic MRI showing early peripheral enhancement with centripetal progression
Hormone profile (including oestrogen) if there are oestrogenic manifestations
Tumour markers such as CA125 mainly to help exclude malignancy
Histology with immunohistochemistry (e.g. inhibin, calretinin) to confirm the sex cord-stromal nature
Endometrial assessment if unopposed oestrogen effects are suspected
redFlags: Menstrual disturbance or oestrogenic symptoms with an adnexal mass requiring endometrial evaluation
Acute pain suggesting torsion of the mass
Imaging or histological features raising doubt about a malignant stromal tumour
A signet-ring-like appearance prompting exclusion of metastatic Krukenberg tumour
reference.prognosis: Excellent, as the tumour is benign and cured by simple excision, with hormonal effects resolving after removal and no established tendency to recur or metastasise.
pitfalls: Mistaking the cellular, vascular histology for a malignant tumour and overtreating a young patient
Confusing signet-ring-like cells with metastatic Krukenberg tumour
Overlooking oestrogenic effects on the endometrium
Performing radical rather than fertility-sparing surgery in a young woman
references: WHO Classification of Female Genital Tumours
Blaustein's Pathology of the Female Genital Tract
